summary: A draft list of ARPANET host names from Richard Watson at the Network Information Center. Starred entries are the names hosts asked for, others are assigned, and the author asks for corrections before a deadline in order to publish an official list.

plainLanguage.summary: A draft list of names for each computer. People can send fixes before the list becomes official.

subtitle: A draft of official names and addresses for ARPANET computers

tldr.problem: The early ARPANET needed a standard way to name and identify the computers (hosts) connected to the network, but there was no consensus yet on what to call them.
tldr.mechanism: Richard Watson at the Network Information Center publishes a draft list of formal host names, nicknames and network addresses, and invites corrections from host representatives before a deadline.
tldr.outcome: This draft became the basis for official ARPANET host naming and the Network Information Center's role as keeper of the official host registry.

today: RFC 280 was a snapshot of the very early ARPANET. It documents the need for and early practice of maintaining a central host registry—a function that evolved into the Domain Name System (DNS) that governs host naming today. The specific names and addresses listed here were superseded long ago, but the principle that networks need a centralized, authoritative registry of host identities remains fundamental.

sections.title: ARPANET Host Names
sections.content: This RFC is a working document from Richard Watson at the Network Information Center (NIC) at SRI-ARC, published in November 1971. It lists the names of computers connected to ARPANET, along with their nicknames and network addresses. The purpose is to collect feedback from host representatives and publish an official registry by December 3, 1971.
sections.plainLanguage: Early ARPANET computers needed official names. This list asks each computer to confirm or correct its entry.

sections.title: Host Names and Addresses
sections.content:
The list shows three pieces of information for each ARPANET host: a formal name (such as MIT-DMCG, or SRI-AI), an optional nickname (such as NIC for SRI-ARC, or CCN for UCLA-CCN), and a numerical network address (for example, SRI-ARC is address 2, BBN-NCC is address 5, and UTAH-10 is address 4). Names with an asterisk were requested by the host itself; others were assigned by the NIC.

The list includes roughly thirty-five hosts, ranging from universities (MIT, Stanford, Harvard) to research institutions (RAND, MITRE) to government labs (NBS, NCAR). Each entry reflects the organization and the type of computer at that site.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer gets a proper name (like MIT-DMCG), possibly a short nickname (like DMCG), and a number (like 70) so it can be found on the network.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content: This RFC marks an important early moment in ARPANET administration: the formalization of a host registry. The list documents what was to become the role of the Network Information Center—keeping the authoritative record of ARPANET hosts and their addresses. Although this particular document is only a draft, it shows the NIC's methods and the effort to bring order to a growing network. The host naming scheme shown here, with formal names linked to network addresses, became a model for how networks would organize and identify their members.
sections.plainLanguage: This is one of the first times anyone officially listed every computer on the network and asked for corrections, starting a tradition of keeping an official registry.
